summary: Details the use of RSVP policy elements that carry application information. Network devices can use this identity data to make policy decisions about a traffic flow. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A traffic request can carry a label saying which program it comes from. Network devices read the label to decide how to treat it.

questions: what is an rsvp application identity policy element
what are app ver and sapp in a policy locator
is the rsvp application policy element secure
subtitle: How an RSVP request can name the application behind it, so network policy can treat a mission-critical program differently from a game.

tldr.problem: Network devices that apply quality-of-service policy to RSVP requests have no standard way to learn which application a reservation is being made for.
tldr.mechanism: An AUTH_APP policy element carries a POLICY_LOCATOR attribute (an X.500 distinguished name built from keywords such as APP, VER and SAPP) plus a CREDENTIAL attribute holding the application name.
tldr.outcome: Administrators can write policy by application type, but the element is only a claim: it is not signed, so it is trusted only as far as the accompanying user policy element is.

today: RFC 2872 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its security section says signed application policy elements may be proposed at a future date.

sections.title: Why Name the Application
sections.content:
RSVP signaling messages (RFC 2205) typically carry policy data objects, and these contain policy elements. Some policy elements describe the user or the application, and RSVP-aware network elements can use that information when deciding how to treat a traffic flow.

RFC 2872 details the use of policy elements that provide application information. Its example is a network administrator who sets a policy that prioritizes known mission-critical applications over games.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school bus driver who lets the fire drill team on first. To do that, the driver needs to know who is who. This RFC is the name tag for programs.

sections.title: Enforcement Points and the Locator Hierarchy
sections.content:
RSVP-aware network elements may act as policy enforcement points (PEPs). A PEP extracts policy information from RSVP signaling requests and compares it with information stored by a policy decision point (PDP) in a possibly remote policy database or directory. The decision is made from the result of that comparison.

The application is described by a policy locator with hierarchically ordered sub-elements, from the top down: an identifier of the application vendor, an identifier of the application, the application version number, and a sub-application identifier. Any number of sub-application identifiers may appear; the RFC's example is print transaction.

The memo specifies the structure and proposes keywords for each level. It does not list specific values for them, which it calls beyond its scope.
sections.eli5: The locator is like a full address: country, city, street, house. It starts with who made the program and gets more specific, down to one small job inside it.

sections.title: The Policy Element Structure
sections.content:
General application identity policy elements are defined in RFC 2752. They have a P-type of AUTH_APP, and the policy element header is followed by a list of authentication attributes.

The first attribute has A-type POLICY_LOCATOR. Its sub-type is ASCII_DN (see RFC 1779) or UNICODE_DN, and its data is an X.500 distinguished name that represents a globally unique identifier, the application, the version number and the sub-application in a hierarchy.

The second attribute has A-type CREDENTIAL. Its sub-type is ASCII_ID or UNICODE_ID, and its data is the application name as a string (the RFC's example is SAP.EXE). The diagram in the RFC shows a PE Length field, the P-type, and then an Attribute Length, A-type and Sub-type for each of the two attributes.
sections.eli5: The tag has two lines. One line is the long, careful address of the program. The other is its everyday file name, like a nickname.

sections.title: Locator Keywords and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC recommends four keywords, although others MAY be used: GUID (globally unique identifier, optional), APP (application name), VER (application version number) and SAPP (sub application, optional).

APP, VER and SAPP SHOULD describe the application to a human reader in as unique and unambiguous a way as possible. GUID MAY be used when absolute uniqueness is required, and its contents MUST be an identifier from a globally unique source, such as domain names assigned by the registration authorities. Publishing the chosen identifiers in a suitable format is strongly encouraged.
sections.eli5: The tag uses short labels: APP for the program, VER for its version, SAPP for a small job inside it, and GUID when you must be sure no one else has the same name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The simple policy element does not guarantee that it really belongs to the application it names. Providing that guarantee would require signed applications, and signed application policy elements may be proposed at a future date.

The application policy element will typically travel in an RSVP message with an encrypted and authenticated user policy element, so a level of security comes from trusting the application element only if the user element is trusted. All RSVP integrity considerations apply to the message containing it.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any name on a name tag. So the network only believes the tag when it already trusts the person wearing it.
